newsitem.title: USA: Five dollar family meals for the holidays.
newsitem.headline: Five dollar family meals for the holidays.

text.p: Around the holidays it's natural to want to splurge, but what you over-spend today, you'll have to pay for tomorrow.

This is especially true when it comes to entertaining. It's very possible, in fact easy, to spend as little as $5 for a festive meal for four without anyone knowing or caring how much you've spent, says a food professional who has made it her business to keep meal prices in the single digits.
"We think of holidays as a time to splurge, but you can also do great food every day on a budget," said Marcie Rothman, aka "The $5 Chef."

Don't think you can run to the supermarket and pick up fixings for a $5 dinner. It takes some planning. The trick is to shop seasonally and avoid those pre-packaged foods that promise to be quick and easy, but are really only expensive.

"No zucchini in the middle of winter. Don't look for tomatoes either," said Rothman, a Sacramento, Calif.-based writer and radio host. Rather, zero in on the winter squashes that are plentiful at this time of year and other vegetables such as broccoli and cauliflower.

A winter squash, at about 69 cents a pound, can be used to make a very festive and unusual squash-curry soup, Rothman said, which is appropriate for any holiday gathering. You don't have to offer a platter of out-of-season tomatoes to be a good host.
One golden rule of food budgeting is using basic ingredients rather than packaged mixes.
"We're seduced, so to speak, by Madison Avenue and the big food makers that (pre-packaged foods) are really convenient," she said.

Rather, a holiday cook on a budget will find that these mixes are nothing more than expensive. A box of herbed rice mix may cost $1.25 for four servings, while a pound of rice, together with spices you already have, may cost far less and produce 16 or more servings.

If you're hosting holiday dinners, it's a wise idea to begin your shopping far in advance, keeping an eye out for staples and other items that last a long time and can be frozen until needed. For example, carrots, potatoes, parsnips and other root vegetables, plentiful and inexpensive this time of year, can be bought in large quantities and can be kept, unrefrigerated in a cool part of your kitchen, for weeks.

Turkeys, a traditional centrepiece of many holiday meals, can be purchased ahead of time when they are on sale if you have a coupon. According to the National Turkey Federation, a turkey can be kept in the freezer, properly wrapped, for up to a year.

Seemingly expensive items, such as fresh mushrooms in small quantities, can take a pedestrian meal and make it festive. You only need a few to add to a salad or gravy and put "a high end item into an otherwise everyday meal," she said.
Staples of holiday baking such as sugar and butter can be bought in bulk and stored.
"Butter, like much dairy, has cyclical prices, so buy when it's on special and buy as much as you can freeze," she said. Butter also lasts in the freezer for months.
Eggs often go up in price around the holidays, but the larger quantities, such as 18, ususally cost less per egg than a dozen. Eggs last three to four weeks in the refrigerator.

Rothman, who has appeared on television as The $5 Chef, offers recipes to help cooks keep to the $5 per meal-for-four ideal, but said, "they're not etched in stone. Recipes should be used as a guide. Use what you have on hand."
"We get so afraid," she said, "that we look at recipes and think it won't work without every single ingredient."

In her new book, "The $5 Chef Family Cookbook" (Prima Publishing, $12, C$16.95), she offers some basic substitutions -- common, inexpensive ingredients you're likely to already have for more esoteric or expensive ones that you may not want to buy.

She writes that instead of honey, you can substitute 1-1/4 cup of sugar plus 1/4 cup liquid; for one teaspoon of lemon juice use 1/2 teaspoon vinegar; or for one ounce (square) of baking chocolate use three tablespoons of cocoa and one tablespoon of butter or oil.
Many families don't consider a meal a meal unless there is meat, but Rothman says as a rule Americans eat far more meat than they require for a healthy diet.
"You don't have to make it a whole steak. You can use meat like a condiment, a side dish almost. It's a much more agreeable way to wean off the great amounts of meat we eat."
Look for meat on sale, slice it thinly, and offer your family and guests each four ounces to six ounces of meat, about the amount that fits in the palm of your hand.
Not only is this an appropriate serving size, it'll also help you on the budget straight and narrow.
